title: ArchPHI
oneLiner: The operating system for architectural drawings. The first piece reads what a drawing declares and writes the bill of quantities.
summary: ArchPHI is building the operating system for architectural drawings — one substrate that reads real CAD deliveries exactly, and a family of construction workflows on top of it. The first workflow is the bill of quantities. Everything rests on one rule: the system only accepts facts it can trace back to the exact CAD, and where a drawing carries no answer, it says so instead of guessing. The corpus behind it is eight real projects; every claim below cites the artifact it comes from.
role: Founder & CTO — I own the architecture, the codebase, and the decision records. My cofounder brings the licensed-professional review.
privateNote: The corpus is real client work under anonymization — eight projects, never named. Quantities, bills, and drawings stay private.

featuredMetric.label: records inventoried in one census of the corpus — every record bucketed exactly once

metrics.label: readable-sheet dimensions yielding a supported geometric measured value
projects in the corpus — 304 files opened, 151 DXF conversions parsed
scored evaluation runs archived, each against a held-out answer key
a no-preparation control beat the staged pipeline on a 39-line bill — the stages stayed unmerged

problem: Real architectural CAD deliveries are messy: nested blocks, references that point at files outside the package, corrupt sheets, dimensions whose displayed text disagrees with their true geometry. Any system that reasons over drawings — takeoff first, everything after it later — produces confident wrong answers unless every fact it accepts can be checked against the exact CAD. The hard problem is not the model. It is a substrate honest enough to keep a model from hallucinating in a domain where wrong numbers cost real money.
constraints: Element vocabulary — door, window, room — must come from each project's own schedules and tags, never from hardcoded modules. Real offices do not share conventions.
Nothing is silently dropped: corrupt drawings and missing references surface as evidence, not as absences.
DWG is not directly parseable; it converts out-of-band to DXF, and the conversion is recorded as provenance rather than assumed lossless.
Corpus numbers are never allowed to overclaim — the census itself states that 74.1% handled does not mean 74.1% understood.
Model calls are priced and capped before they are ever wired in.

approach.decision: Made 'element types are evidence, not code' an executable law — an AST gate fails the build if an element-named identifier appears in foundation code.
approach.why: Hardcoding one office's conventions is how a system stops generalizing. A build failure cannot quietly erode.

approach.decision: Built an exact-CAD extraction substrate instead of computer vision: nested blocks expanded into world-space primitives with full ancestry, and content-based IDs that survive re-extraction.
approach.why: Vector structure — geometry, text, dimensions, provenance — is a richer ground truth than pixels, and stable IDs let a later reasoner cite and re-verify a fact after unrelated edits.

approach.decision: Censused the entire corpus once: 2,668,953 records across eight projects, each bucketed exactly once as handled, raw-reachable, or unsupported.
approach.why: You cannot claim coverage you have not counted. The census also documents what its numbers are not — presence in this corpus is not presence in general.

approach.decision: Evaluated against held-out answer keys: sessions receive a deliberately sparse bill, the key is never shown, and scores land in six mutually exclusive buckets that sum to the bill length.
approach.why: Flagging must not look like accuracy and guessing must not look like coverage. Seventeen runs are archived under that scheme.

approach.decision: Deleted work that did not survive its own evidence — a prior pipeline that was semantically mute on 12 of 16 real sheets, and staged preparation that a no-preparation control beat 22 to 16 on a 39-line bill.
approach.why: Sophistication that does not generalize is a liability. The failure evidence is written down, not hidden.

implementation: The extraction substrate over DXF (ezdxf): nested INSERT/MINSERT blocks expanded to world space with full ancestry, OCS-to-WCS transforms, and content-based IDs stable across re-extraction.

A content-hashed ingestion boundary that types every delivered file into one of four evidence tiers, links DWG-to-DXF conversions as provenance, and surfaces corrupt drawings instead of dropping them.
A reference census that marks every declared image, underlay, XREF, and font present or missing — one real sheet declared 21 external images, all pointing outside the package, all flagged.

Dimension evidence read from true geometry rather than displayed text: 766 of 766 readable-sheet dimensions yield a supported measured value, with 13 explicit text-overrides surfaced rather than silently trusted.
The corpus census machinery: 304 files opened once, 2,668,953 records bucketed exactly once — 74.1% handled, 25.8% raw-reachable, 0.03% unsupported.
The evaluation harness: sparse bills in, answer keys isolated, six-bucket scoring out; 17 scored runs archived with per-run records.
A diagnosis of area measurement that names its root cause — 1 of 14 lines correct across 42 attempts, because vertical area needs a height the drawings do not carry.

outcomes.label: One census opened every drawing in the corpus and bucketed every record exactly once
Every readable-sheet dimension yields a supported geometric measured value
A no-preparation control outscored the staged pipeline, so the stages were never merged
Area measurement failed and the failure is diagnosed to a named root cause, not averaged away
The interpretation layer stays unshipped until the verification spine can check its claims — a decision, not a gap

stack: ODA File Converter (DWG→DXF, behind a provenance seam)
limitations: 74.1% of records handled does not mean 74.1% of a drawing understood — the census says so itself, and so do I.
No product accuracy number is claimed anywhere; the evaluation scheme exists precisely because one honest number does not exist yet.
The quantity-takeoff workflow the substrate serves is not shipped. First firms are onboarding soon.
DWG quality is bounded by the out-of-band converter until a first-party path exists.
Area measurement is unsolved: 1 of 14 lines correct across 42 attempts, root cause named — the drawings do not carry the height the computation needs.

title: PiloneCables
category: Search platform for a cable manufacturer · pilonecables.com
oneLiner: A factory's site rebuilt into 288 pages that rank — organic clicks up 5.2× in six months, average position 17.8 → 8.4.
summary: Pilone manufactures electrical cable in Pakistan. I build and run their website: product pages, guides, and sizing calculators generated from factory data. When I took it on it had roughly 65 indexed pages and sat at position 13 for the queries that mattered. Six months of measured work later, organic clicks are up 5.2×, average position moved from 17.8 to 8.4, and the site went from invisible to AI search to 3.87k impressions in three months. The part I keep: at one point the pipeline generated over a thousand pages, and the right move was deleting 405 of them.
role: Sole builder and operator — the site, the build pipeline, the content system, and the search work.

featuredMetric.label: organic clicks, six months vs the prior six — 5.2×

metrics.label: average position in Google Search over the same window
impressions in AI search, three months
URLs in the live sitemap — 96 product, 89 guides, 70 city pages, plus tools
clicks and average position at the January baseline, before the overhaul

problem: A cable factory sells through distributors and word of mouth; buyers search by product, size, and price and find the established brands instead. The site had ~65 indexed pages, no answers to the questions people actually type, and no way for the factory's real advantage — its own data — to reach a search result.
constraints: Factory data is the source of truth — prices and specifications change, so pages regenerate from data rather than being hand-edited.
Volume without quality backfires: mass-generated pages had to earn their place or be cut.
AI assistants now answer buyer questions directly, so the site had to be legible to their crawlers, not just to Google.
One person runs this alongside everything else — the pipeline has to keep the site correct without daily attention.

approach.decision: Generate pages from the factory's data — a product × size × guide matrix with structured data on every page.
approach.why: The factory's own specifications and prices are what buyers search for, and no competitor can copy data it does not have.

approach.decision: Prune hard: of 1,053 generated pages, 405 thin ones were deleted and 236 became redirects, leaving 288 that earn their rank.
approach.why: Search rewards a site where every page answers something. The deletion moved the numbers, not the generation.

approach.decision: Build tools buyers actually use — a cable-size calculator and a voltage-drop calculator, with conversion events on both.
approach.why: A calculator answers the question a spec table cannot, and its usage shows up in analytics as intent, not traffic.

approach.decision: Make the site legible to AI search: llms.txt, an AI-crawler allowlist, and clean structured data.
approach.why: Buyers increasingly ask an assistant instead of Google. Three months after the work: 3.87k impressions in AI search, from zero.

approach.decision: Measure everything in Search Console and let the numbers pick the next move.
approach.why: Position and clicks are the only verdict that matters here — the work iterates against them, not against opinions.

implementation: A static multi-page site (Vite) where every page is generated from factory data at build time.
A 19-script build pipeline: price sync, navigation injection, search index, sitemap, llms.txt, and redirect stubs.
Cable-size and voltage-drop calculators plus ampacity, wire-size, and copper-weight reference charts.
Client-side search over a 288-entry index.
GA4 with custom events for contact clicks and calculator use.
Deployed on Render behind Cloudflare, from a repo I have committed to for over a year.

outcomes.label: Organic clicks, six months vs the prior six
Average position in Google Search
Impressions in AI search, three months, from a standing start
Click-through rate over the same six-month window

limitations: Impressions grew 9.92k → 46.2k in the same window, but part of that range sits inside a documented Search Console logging-error period — clicks and position are the series I trust, so they lead.
Sitemap URLs are not the same as indexed pages; I do not claim an indexed count.
Growth attribution is observational — there was no controlled experiment, just a baseline, the work, and the after.

title: TalentFlow
oneLiner: Recruitment end to end: five candidate sources into one semantic pipeline, and a conversational agent that runs the first interview. Built by four engineers I led.
summary: TalentFlow replaces keyword CV screening with retrieval: a candidate's public footprint — CV, GitHub, LinkedIn, ORIC, personal site — is ingested, embedded with Nomic into Weaviate, and matched against LLM-enhanced job descriptions by meaning rather than keyword overlap. On top sits the interview agent, built as a loop: an orchestrator with windowed memory picks the next topic, a two-stage generator writes a question that avoids template phrasing, TTS speaks it, the candidate answers, Whisper transcribes, and the transcript feeds the next turn. On conclude, a report engine scores the session. I led the four-person team and owned the architecture, over a fixed summer internship.
role: Team lead — four engineers, architecture owned end to end.
privateNote: Internal research-lab build over personal data — described by architecture, never by candidates.

featuredMetric.label: engineers led, architecture owned end to end

metrics.label: candidate sources ingested — CV, GitHub, LinkedIn, ORIC, personal site
question generation — a draft pass, then a strict-JSON pass that rejects template phrasing
interview-agent response on Groq-served Llama 3, as reported — not an audited benchmark

problem: Manual screening is slow and shallow: recruiters skim CVs and miss the context spread across a candidate's GitHub, LinkedIn, and personal site. The lab wanted the whole first pass automated — assemble the footprint, match it to a role by meaning, and run a conversational first-round interview that does not repeat itself.
constraints: A fixed internship window to ship end to end with a team of four.
Heterogeneous, personal input data — five sources with five structures, all carrying PII.
Lab servers, not managed cloud — deployment had to be self-hosted and reproducible.
A conversational interview is a state problem: low latency, no repeated questions, coherent topic progression.
Small open models only — Llama 3 on Groq, not frontier APIs.

approach.decision: Semantic retrieval over keyword filtering: Nomic embeddings in Weaviate, matching candidates and roles in one vector space.
approach.why: Fit lives in context and phrasing that keyword filters miss.

approach.decision: Enhance job descriptions with an LLM before embedding them.
approach.why: Raw job posts are terse and inconsistent; normalizing them first gives retrieval a comparable vector on both sides.

approach.decision: Build the interviewer as a loop of small parts — orchestrator, topic selection, two-stage question generation, TTS, STT — instead of one looping prompt.
approach.why: Non-repetition and topic progression are state management. The orchestrator keeps windowed memory, checks for gaps every two questions, and votes on ending every five.

approach.decision: Serve the loop on Llama 3 via Groq.
approach.why: Conversation needs low latency, and fast inference on a small model beat slow inference on a large one for this loop.

approach.decision: Split ingestion, embedding, matching, and interviewing into containerized services with async jobs.
approach.why: The stages have different runtime shapes, and Docker Compose made the whole pipeline reproducible on lab hardware.

implementation: Multi-source ingestion that scrapes and normalizes candidate data from five sources into structured JSON.
Nomic embeddings indexed in Weaviate for candidate-job matching, with LLM-enhanced job descriptions.
The interview loop: orchestrator with windowed memory and gap checks, two-stage anti-template question generation, TTS voice out, Whisper transcription back.
A report engine that runs on conclude: audio features extracted from the session plus parallel scoring over the transcript.
A FastAPI backend with async job processing, deployed as containerized microservices on lab servers.

outcomes.label: Led four engineers and owned the platform architecture end to end
Interview agent responds in under five seconds without repeating questions, as reported
The first screening pass runs without a human in the loop; no measured screening-time percentage is claimed

limitations: Match quality was never benchmarked — no precision or recall was measured, so the retrieval win is architectural, not proven.
The sub-5s figure is reported from one Groq-served setup, not audited.
It is a lab prototype: before real candidates it would need consent, retention limits, and access controls that were out of scope for the internship.
An 8B model bounds interview judgment; a production system would evaluate against stronger models first.

title: Revvy
oneLiner: Ingests a business's Google reviews at scale and drafts on-brand replies for an operator to approve — with the throughput and cost work documented.
summary: Revvy connects to Google Business Profile over OAuth, syncs reviews, and generates per-location reply drafts an operator approves and publishes. Each workspace picks how much runs unattended: manual, draft-then-approve, or auto-post above a star threshold. The engineering story is throughput and cost — pre-filtering that skips ineligible reviews before any model call, three generation strategies matched to the job, batched writes, and tagged caching. The numbers below come from the project's own PERFORMANCE.md.
role: Sole builder — data model, OAuth layer, background jobs, generation pipeline, dashboard.
privateNote: Built for a client; no connected accounts, business names, or review text are ever shown.

featuredMetric.label: faster large syncs — 2,000 reviews from ~60–120 min sequential to ~10–20 min parallel

metrics.label: cached page loads, down from 300–1,000ms
database queries per full sync after write batching
generation cost cut by pre-filtering ineligible reviews before any model call

problem: A business with many locations accumulates reviews faster than anyone can read, draft, and post replies. The naive automation is worse: a sequential sync of a few thousand reviews takes over an hour, and generating a reply for every review spends model budget on reviews that are already answered or never needed one.
constraints: Live customer data under Google's platform terms — nothing identifying leaves the system.
Access tokens expire mid-sync and refresh grants get permanently revoked; the integration has to tell those apart.
Model calls cost money per review and rate limits are real.
Multi-tenant from day one — every workspace's locations, prompts, and caches stay isolated.
No extra infrastructure: the job queue had to live in the database already in the stack.

approach.decision: Pre-filter before generating: skip reviews already replied to, below threshold, or already drafted.
approach.why: The cheapest model call is the one that never happens — the filter is where the cost discipline comes from.

approach.decision: Three generation strategies instead of one code path: parallel for small syncs, throttled for rate-limit safety, and the Batch API for cheap bulk work.
approach.why: Throughput, cost, and latency trade against each other; one path cannot serve all three.

approach.decision: A real OAuth lifecycle: refresh with an expiry buffer, cache tokens per request, and treat invalid_grant as a dead connection, not a retry.
approach.why: Long syncs outlive tokens, and a revoked grant loops forever if the code cannot tell it from a transient failure.

approach.decision: pg-boss for jobs, so the queue is a Postgres table instead of a second system.
approach.why: One fewer thing to operate mattered more than a marginally faster broker.

approach.decision: Batch writes in transactions and cache read-heavy pages with per-workspace invalidation.
approach.why: The hidden bottleneck was ~2,000 individual queries per sync, not the model.

implementation: Google Business Profile integration on NextAuth with offline access and a token layer that survives expiry mid-sync.
Review ingestion that paginates the API and batch-upserts into Postgres inside transactions.
A reply pipeline with per-location prompts, business context injection, and first-name-only personalization.
The three-mode automation model — manual, draft-then-approve, auto-post at or above a per-location star threshold.
Background jobs on pg-boss: sync, generate, and post as typed handlers, plus a Pub/Sub endpoint for near-real-time triggers.
The operator dashboard: connect, locations, and an inbox to generate, edit, approve, and publish.

outcomes.label: 2,000-review sync, sequential vs parallel
Cached reviews and locations pages
Database queries per full sync after batching
Generation spend cut by filtering ineligible reviews before any call

limitations: The numbers are the project's own benchmarks from PERFORMANCE.md, not audited production metrics.
Per-location voice memory is scaffolded but not in the shipped loop — reply voice comes from prompts and injected context.
Auto-post above a threshold exists, but I would want reply-quality evaluation in place before trusting it more broadly.

title: Emmy
oneLiner: Sorts a business inbox into its own categories as native Gmail labels — known senders routed by rule, everything ambiguous classified with thread context, every decision logged with its reasoning.
summary: Emmy sorts incoming Gmail into a client's own categories and applies each decision as a real Gmail label, near-real-time. The design is two layers: deterministic contact-group rules resolve known senders with zero model cost, and a thread-aware LLM handles the rest using full conversation context, the owner's To/CC/BCC role, and the client's past corrections. New mail arrives through a Gmail Pub/Sub webhook into a background job, and every categorization is persisted with a structured reasoning log — who sent it, how it was addressed, what category, and why — visible in the dashboard. It runs on real inboxes as client work and ships on the Simplabots platform.
role: Sole builder — pipeline, prompting, Gmail integration, dashboard.
privateNote: Runs over real client inboxes — architecture is public, inbox content never is.

featuredMetric.label: model calls for known senders — single-category contact groups route by rule

metrics.label: structured reasoning log — sender, To/CC/BCC role, category, and the model's reasoning, stored and shown
configurable initial ingest, chosen in the setup wizard
the Batch API — up to 24h latency is wrong for an inbox that should feel live

problem: A client needed incoming mail sorted into their operational categories, inside the inbox they already use — not another app. Sending every message to a model is slow, expensive, and drifts within conversations; pure rules cannot handle the mail that actually needs judgment. And when the system gets one wrong, the fix has to teach it.
constraints: Near-real-time: new mail gets labeled promptly or the sorting is useless.
Real inboxes — tokens and message bodies stay server-side, always.
Known senders must never cost a model call.
A thread split across categories is worse than no sorting at all.
Corrections have to change future behavior without a retraining pipeline.

approach.decision: Two layers: contact-group rules first, the model only for what rules cannot resolve.
approach.why: Known senders are the common case. Matching sender or domain to a single-category group short-circuits with zero cost, so the model budget goes where judgment is actually needed.

approach.decision: Classify threads, not messages.
approach.why: The classifier reads the conversation and keeps it in one category; moving one message re-routes the thread. Per-message drift is the failure users notice first.

approach.decision: Structured context instead of raw text: the owner's To/CC/BCC role, internal vs external domain, reply and forward signals, and per-category descriptions — with a strict-JSON contract and a safe fallback on any parse failure.
approach.why: Concrete signals make the output consistent enough to automate; the contract makes failure safe instead of silent.

approach.decision: Corrections feed forward: the last ten corrections are injected into subsequent prompts.
approach.why: The client's real conventions show up immediately, with no training loop to own.

approach.decision: Contact groups do double duty: CRUD with bulk email import, and multi-category assignment that drives auto-routing.
approach.why: The client's own address book is the best classifier there is — the model should only see what it cannot answer.

implementation: The ingestion path: Gmail Pub/Sub webhook, decoded into a background job (Inngest) that categorizes in small batches and applies labels.
The deterministic layer: sender and domain matching against contact groups, with single-category groups short-circuiting.
The classification prompt and strict-JSON contract, tuned for deterministic single-pass output.
Label writes through a manager that can also restore everything to the inbox on account deletion — uninstalling leaves the inbox clean.
The reasoning log: structured JSON per email — sender, addressed-to role, category, reasoning — persisted and surfaced in a dashboard modal.
The dashboard: category manager, contact-group CRUD with bulk import, setup wizard with configurable ingest, and a thread-grouped inbox view.

outcomes.label: Known senders route with zero model cost, by construction
Every categorization is auditable in-product: structured reasoning plus confidence, per email
Shipped configurable initial ingest (100–1,000 emails) and contact groups with bulk import driving auto-routing
Runs commercially — Emmy is live as an agent on the Simplabots platform

limitations: Confidence scores are a heuristic that flags fallbacks — they are not calibrated probabilities.
Some ambiguous mail is left uncategorized on purpose; a human deciding is the correct outcome for those.
An embedding layer is scaffolded in the schema but the shipped path is rules plus prompt — I would measure whether vectors earn their place before wiring them in.

title: MelodyMind
oneLiner: Emotion-aware playlists from text, images, and voice — built on a frozen CLAP audio encoder aligned to a text embedding space, a design reached only after the naive baselines collapsed.
summary: MelodyMind generates playlists from what you say, type, or show it. The research core is cross-modal alignment: a frozen CLAP audio encoder projected through a trained head into the same latent space as Nomic text embeddings, aligned with an InfoNCE contrastive loss. That design was not the first idea — it came after spectrogram CNNs and text-sentiment baselines collapsed, and after a structured zero-shot evaluation mapped exactly where the pretrained model fails. The model was then productized over three iterations into a working prototype: text, image, and voice playlist generation, a real-time talk-to-your-DJ voice loop, and stem separation — served by FastAPI and Pinecone, with a React Native app. Thesis work, built by a team of three.
role: One of three builders (with Hassaan Anwar and Saad Nadeem). The thesis does not attribute modules to individuals, so this page describes shared work.

featuredMetric.label: to stable embedding separation — the feature collapse of the earlier baselines, eliminated

metrics.label: builders — team thesis at FAST-NUCES
zero-shot emotion probes mapping where pretrained CLAP succeeds and fails
iterations — embedding research, multimodal productization, stem separation

problem: Emotional intent lives in text — 'something for a rainy focus session' — while the signal lives in audio, and the two have no shared representation. The first attempts made that concrete: sentiment classifiers over lyrics, spectrogram CNNs, concatenated pipelines — all collapsed into embeddings that did not separate by emotion. The real question became how to align audio and text into one space reliably enough to recommend across modalities.
constraints: No labeled emotion-to-audio ground truth — training data assembled from public sources with real class imbalance.
Audio limited to short public previews, not full tracks.
Three people, a fixed academic timeline.
No compute to train an audio encoder — the design had to lean on a frozen pretrained one.

approach.decision: Freeze CLAP and train only a small projection head into the Nomic text space.
approach.why: It reuses CLAP's audio understanding and reduces the problem to one learnable projection — the tractable path with no ground-truth dataset and no training budget.

approach.decision: Align with an InfoNCE in-batch contrastive loss rather than regression or classification.
approach.why: Contrastive pairing optimizes audio-text matching and song-to-song discrimination at once — which is what fixed the collapse.

approach.decision: Run a structured zero-shot evaluation before committing to training: ten emotion prompts against pretrained CLAP.
approach.why: It showed exactly where the model is strong (direct emotions, tempo, timbre) and weak (abstract cues like 'focus') — evidence for the projection head, not an assumption.

approach.decision: Serve recommendation as vector geometry: weighted centroids in Pinecone with mood filtering by distance.
approach.why: Once the modalities share a space, playlists reduce to geometry and the serving path stays inspectable.

approach.decision: Route conversation through Gemini with a Llama-on-Groq fallback.
approach.why: The voice loop needs to stay responsive when the primary model is slow.

implementation: The projection head mapping frozen CLAP audio embeddings into the Nomic text dimensionality, trained with InfoNCE.
The naive baselines that failed first — lyric and Reddit sentiment classifiers, spectrogram CNNs — kept as the documented reason for the design.
A data pipeline over Reddit, Last.fm, Genius lyrics, and Deezer previews with concurrent download and feature extraction.
A FastAPI backend with async SQLAlchemy, embeddings served from Pinecone with centroid-based playlist construction.
The talk-to-your-DJ loop: voice in, Whisper transcript, an agent that updates the playlist mid-session, streamed spoken reply.
Image-to-playlist via multimodal mood extraction mapped to embedding queries.
Demucs-based stem separation with an async job lifecycle and downloadable stems.
The React Native app: chat playlists, image upload, the animated voice screen, stem upload and preview — verified on real devices.

outcomes.label: The CLAP-InfoNCE model stabilized with clear embedding separation, eliminating the baselines' feature collapse
The zero-shot evaluation documented strengths and weaknesses honestly — a diagnosis used to justify the design, not a headline
A working multimodal prototype: text, image, and voice playlist generation plus the voice loop, on real devices
End-to-end stem separation shipped in the final iteration — vocals, drums, bass, and other, downloadable

limitations: No recommendation-quality benchmark was measured — no accuracy, MAP, or nDCG. The honest next step is a held-out evaluation against a labeled set.
The encoder stays weak on abstract, situational prompts; closing that needs targeted data, not more epochs.
It is a research demonstrator, not a launched app — some integrations were finished only in the last iteration.
Training data came from public sources with real imbalance and preview-length audio.
